segments.text: All right team, we have 8 weeks until the Peking Humanoid World Cup. Let's review what needs to be built and fixed.
Thomas, as Product Owner, give us the priorities. What are the must-haves for the competition?

The humanoid league has strict requirements. First, the robots need to walk stably on natural grass, not just artificial turf. Second, we need ball handling while walking, not just standing. Third, the fall recovery has to work within 5 seconds per the rules.
Anna, how's the gait controller? Can we handle grass yet?
The ZMP-based gait works on turf, but grass is unpredictable. The foot sinks differently each step. We need terrain adaptation, probably a compliance controller for the ankle joints.
That's a significant feature. What's the complexity estimate?

High complexity. We're talking about integrating IMU feedback with joint torque sensors, then training a policy to adjust step height in real-time. I'd estimate 3 weeks minimum, and we need access to a grass field for testing.
Markus, can we get grass field test time?
The local stadium rents out a training pitch. I can book 4-hour slots on Tuesdays and Thursdays. We'll need to transport the robots and the calibration rig.
Book it for the next 6 weeks. We need at least 12 sessions to validate the grass walking. Anna, that's your primary task.
What about ball handling while walking? Stefan, you've been working on the dribbling controller.

Right now dribbling requires the robot to stand still for at least 200 milliseconds to lock onto the ball. Walking while dribbling drifts the ball away within 3-4 steps. The closed-loop control isn't fast enough.
So we need a predictive controller that anticipates footstep impacts. That touches the walking engine and the vision module.
I've prototyped a model predictive controller in simulation. It keeps the ball within 30 centimeters during continuous walking. But I need Julia's help with the vision latency.
Julia, the ball detection has a 40 millisecond latency. Can we bring that down?

The latency comes from the YOLO inference on the Jetson. We can optimize by reducing the input resolution and running a lighter model. I estimate we can get to 20 milliseconds with some accuracy trade-off.
Do it. 20 milliseconds should be fast enough for the predictive controller. Stefan, what's the estimate for the walking dribble feature?
Medium complexity. Controller is 1 week, integration with vision is 3 days, testing on grass is another week. So about 2.5 weeks total, but it depends on Anna's gait controller being stable first.
That's a dependency we need to track. Anna's terrain adaptation is critical path, Stefan's walking dribble depends on it.
The third must-have is fall recovery within 5 seconds. Lisa, you've been working on the getup motions.
We have recovery sequences from supine and prone positions. The problem is the robot often falls into awkward orientations, like sideways against the goal post. Standard getup motions fail there.
We need context-aware recovery. The robot has to detect obstacles around it and choose a getup strategy that doesn't hit the goal or other robots.
Is that solvable in 8 weeks?

I can build a decision tree based on the torso IMU orientation and the lidar proximity. Three main strategies: forward getup, backward getup, and roll-then-getup. Low complexity, about 5 days including testing.
Good. Mark that as high priority. Now let's talk about fixes for existing bugs.
The wireless latency spikes during matches are critical. Last tournament we had 200 millisecond delays that made teleoperation unusable.
That's the 5GHz band congestion in stadiums. We need to fallback to 2.4GHz automatically when the primary link degrades.
I've written the handoff logic. But the issue is the antenna placement. The omni-directional antenna behind the battery pack gets shielded when the robot leans forward.
We need a mast antenna on the shoulder. That's a hardware change. Markus, can we get custom antenna mounts fabricated?
I'll contact the machine shop. It's a simple 3D-printed part with a cable channel. We can have 6 units ready by next week.
Great. Michael, you own the network stack. Add the automatic band switching and integrate with the new antenna hardware.
Got it. Also there's a bug in the battery management system. The state of charge estimation drifts by 15 percent after extended walking. We shut down early in the second half of matches.
That's the coulomb counting without temperature compensation. The cells heat up during fast walking and the voltage curve shifts.
We need kalman filtering with temperature input. There's a BMS chip that does this, but it requires firmware changes. Can we get that done in time?
Medium complexity. The SOC algorithm is well documented. I can implement it in 3 days, but we need a full battery discharge test for calibration. That's 4 hours of robot runtime.
Schedule the discharge test for this weekend. We can't afford to lose power during matches.
Another critical fix. The vision system loses track of the ball in direct sunlight. The exposure compensation doesn't respond fast enough when robots move from shadow to sun.
The camera auto-exposure has a fixed adaptation rate. We need to override it with a lookup table based on sun position and robot heading.
I'll build an exposure model using the GPS time and the robot's compass. It can predict when the robot is facing the sun and pre-adjust.
That's smart. Low complexity, about 2 days. Make it part of the vision pipeline cleanup.
Now enhancements. The rulebook allows for 4 substitute robots. We should prepare backup units that can swap in quickly.
We have 6 functional robots. Two are competition-ready, two are development units, and two have damaged hip servos.
The hip servos are backordered. I repaired one unit with a 3D-printed gearbox housing. It works but I wouldn't trust it for a full match.
Use it as a substitute. The rules allow 30 seconds for a robot swap. If a primary unit goes down, we need a hot spare ready to go.
I'll set up a pit crew protocol. One technician per robot, standardized startup sequence. We can swap in under 20 seconds with practice.
One more enhancement. The strategy engine currently runs high-level plays. But against strong opponents, we need to adapt mid-game.
We could add a game state analyzer. It recognizes opponent formations and suggests counter-strategies. That's an ML model trained on past match footage.
Do we have enough training data? We've recorded 14 matches over the last two seasons.
That's marginal. We'd need to augment with simulation data. I can generate synthetic matches using our AI playing against itself.
That's a nice-to-have, not a must-have. Lower priority. Thomas, do we commit to building the game state analyzer?
Make it a stretch goal. If Anna and Stefan finish early, they can help with the synthetic data generation. But the three must-haves come first.
Let's recap the commitments. Anna owns terrain adaptation for grass, 3 weeks, critical path. Stefan owns walking dribble, depends on Anna, 2.5 weeks.
Lisa owns fall recovery, 5 days. Michael owns network handoff and battery SOC fix. Julia optimizes vision latency. Markus handles hardware and logistics.
We need a decision documented. The grass field testing requires robot transport and calibration equipment. We should write an ADR for the compliance controller approach.
I'll draft the ADR this week. It should cover the sensor fusion architecture and the training protocol for the grass adaptation policy.
Also note the dependency chain. If grass testing gets delayed by weather, Stefan's ball handling work is blocked. We need an indoor backup plan.
There's an indoor turf facility 30 minutes away. I'll book that as a backup for rainy days. It's not perfect but it keeps the schedule.
Good contingency planning. Let's put all of this on the Jira board. I want to see 4 sprints mapped out with clear dependencies.
Sprint 1 is the foundation. Anna starts grass gait, Julia reduces vision latency, Michael fixes the network stack. Lisa begins fall recovery.
Sprint 2, Anna continues, Stefan integrates the predictive dribble controller. Hardware changes for antenna go in.
Sprint 3 is integration testing. Full matches on grass, battery endurance tests, pit crew drills.
Sprint 4 is polish and travel prep. Final bug fixes, documentation for the technical inspection, spare parts inventory.
One last thing. The technical inspection checklist has 23 items. We need all robots to pass before the first match.
I'll prepare a checklist and run each robot through it. Last year we failed on the battery containment rule. We need to document the safety foam installation.
Add that to the documentation task. We have 8 weeks, let's make them count. This is our shot at the podium.
